Dynamics of piecewise translation maps

Sang Truong

University of California, Irvine

arXiv:1610.04700v2 [math.DS] 19 Aug 2017

July 10, 2018

# Abstract

In this paper, we introduce a generalized piecewise translation map on the Euclidean

space. We provide a special case when this map is always of ﬁnite type. For a ﬁnite

type map in this case, we form conjectures on the semi-continuity of the attractor.

Moreover, we also provide some conjectures and pictures on piecewise translations on

a two dimensional torus.

# 1 Background

The goal of this paper is to study the dynamics of piecewise translation maps. These maps are special types of piecewise isometries on a region Ωin the Euclidean space. To deﬁne piecewise isometries, we partition Ωinto smaller regions P0, · · · , Pm such that these pieces

intersect only at their boundaries. We also assume that the boundary of each piece has zero Lebesgue measure. A map f : Ω → Ωis called a piecewise isometry if the restriction of f

to any piece Pi is an isometry, i.e. it preserves distance on each piece. Piecewise isometries, especially piecewise translation maps, serve as models for many engineering applications, such as the second order digital ﬁlter [6, 7], the sigma-delta modulator [3, 8, 10], the buck converter [7, 9], the three-capacitance model [16], error diﬀusion in digital printing [1, 2], and machine learning.

One of the simplest examples of such piecewise translation can be formed using interval exchange transformations (IET). These transformations are a generalization of a classical dynamical system – circle rotation. To deﬁne an IET, let Ω= [0, 1) ⊆ R be partitioned into

a ﬁnite number of distinct intervals. The map f : Ω → Ωthat permutes the intervals deﬁnes

a piecewise isometry.

Several nice properties of IET have been discovered. In particular, M. Kean [14] showed that every orbit of f is dense in [0, 1). He also proved that if the partition has only two or three

intervals, then all minimal IETs are also uniquely ergodic. The statement is not necessarily true if the number of intervals exceeds 3. However, it was proven by Masur [15] and Veech [20] that almost every interval exchange transformation is uniquely ergodic. This motivates a generalized conjecture that most piecewise isometries (restriction to the attractors) are also uniquely ergodic.

We can also consider a variation of interval exchange transformations, namely interval translation mappings (ITM). These mappings are introduced by M. Boshernitzan and I. Kornfeld in 1995 [5]. For ITM, the images of the intervals are not required to be disjoint. We classify ITM into two types: ﬁnite and inﬁnite. In the case f(Ω) ̸= Ω, consider the sequence

Ω0 = Ω, Ω1 = f(Ω0), . . .. From this, we get the nested chain Ω0 ⊇ Ω1 ⊇ . . .. If this chain

stabilizes we say the map f : Ω → Ωis of ﬁnite type; otherwise, f is of inﬁnite type. We

see that the map can only be of inﬁnite type if there are more than two elements in the partition. In particular, Boshernitzan and Kornﬁeld constructed an ITM of inﬁnite type with three branches [5].

Another class of one dimensional piecewise isometries is the double rotations of the circle. Let Ω= S1 = [0, 1]/{0 ∼1} be partitioned into two arcs P0 and P1. We deﬁne the double

rotation map f : S1 → S1 as following:

f(x) =  x + α0 (mod 1),

if x ∈ P0;

x + α1 (mod 1), if x ∈ P1.

Almost all double rotations of the circle are uniquely ergodic, even most of those of inﬁnite type [4]. We would like to emphasize that this text is the result of an undergraduate research

Each Bi is called a branch of Ω. Locally, if x is in both Bi and Bj, then x will be translated by both vi and vj. Figure 2 represents a piecewise translation of 3 branches on a 2-dimensional disk. These three branches intersect only at their boundaries, which have zero Lebesgue measure. Figure 2 is a simpliﬁed model of machine learning. In order for the machine to learn, we need multiple inputs from the environment. Each input is represented by a translation vector. The process of machine learning is modeled by the dynamics of applying the piecewise translation map many times. Therefore, it is natural to deﬁne what we get after applying the map over and over again, which we will call the attractor.

# 3 Finiteness theorem when m = d + 1

In this section, we are interested in piecewise translation maps of m = d + 1 branches in Rd. We assume that rank{v0, v1, . . . , vm−1} = d; that is, the vectors in B = {v1 − v0, v2 −

4

v0, . . . , vm−1 − v0} form a basis for Rd. Let L be the lattice generated by B, then T = Rd/L

is a d-dimensional torus. In this case, v0 serves as the translation vector in T; i.e. we have the torus rotation map R : T → T, R(x+L) = x+v0 +L. Atom-wise, the action of F is the

same as the action of R on T. Globally, it is also true and can be seen through the canonical projection π : Rd → T, π(x) = x + L.

Lemma 3.1. If K ⊆ Ωis compact, then π ◦ F(K) = R ◦ π(K).

Proof. Let φ ∈ π ◦ T(K), then φ ∈ Sm−1

i=1 π(Ti(Bi ∩ K)). So φ = π(Tj(Bj ∩ K)) for some j.

Therefore, ∃y ∈ Bj ∩ K such that φ = π(y + vj). As a result,

φ = y + vj + L = y + v0 + (vj − v0) + L = y + v0 + L = R ◦ π(y) ∈ R ◦ π(K).

For the backward inclusion, let φ ∈ R◦π(K), then φ = R◦π(y) = y+v0+L for some y ∈ K.

Without loss of generality, we can assume y ∈ Bj. In this case, φ = π(y+vj) ∈ π(Tj(Bj∩K)).

Hence, x ∈ π ◦ F(K).

It was proven that any piecewise translation of an interval with 2 branches is of ﬁnite type [18]. However, this does not hold for dimension 2 or higher. Indeed, not all double rotation on a torus is of ﬁnite type. In the case where m = d + 1, there is a space of parameters (translation vectors) where we will get ﬁnite type attractors. We assume that the translation vectors v0, v1, . . . , vm−1 are rationally independent, i.e. they are linearly independent in

Q-vector space. This is equivalent for the toral map R to be ergodic. In this case, we say that the translation vectors are minimal. With this assumption, the map F is necessarily of ﬁnite type. We start with some deﬁnitions that will be used in the proof.

Deﬁnition 3.1. A set X is said to be invariant under the map f : M → M if f(X) = X.

Deﬁnition 3.2. A toral map R : T → T is said to be minimal if every orbit is dense; i.e

there is no proper closed invariant subset.

Deﬁnition 3.3. A set X ⊆ Rd is nowhere dense if int ¯A = ∅.

Theorem 3.1. Piecewise translation maps with rationally independent translation vectors are of ﬁnite type.

Proof. The idea is to show that F N(Ω) is contained in some ε-neighborhood of A but not contained in ε-neighborhood of ∂A for some N > 0. In this case, F N(Ω) must be in the interior of A, thus a subset of A.

Since A is compact, non-empty and π is continuous, π(A) is compact and non-empty. Moreover, R ◦ π(A) = π ◦ F(A) = π(A) by Lemma 2.1, so π(A) is invariant under R. We know

# 4 Semi-continuity of the attractors

In general, it is not true that the attractor is continuous with respect to Hausdorﬀmetric in the parameter space. Even in the case m = d + 1, we observed that sometimes the two separate pieces of the attractor reglue to each other. One of our concerns has not been proven yet.

Question 4.1. Is it true that for a generic family of partitions, the attractor depends continuously on the translation vectors?

However, in the case m = d + 1, the question of semi-continuity of the attractor is easier to answer. We will show that for a particular family of partitions, ﬁnite type attractors are semi-continuous on the translation vectors. Before showing the proof for this, we need a formal deﬁnition for semi-continuity of the attractors.

Deﬁnition 4.1. Let W be the space of translation vectors such that the associated piecewise

translation map Fv0,v1,...,vm−1 is of ﬁnite type with a ﬁxed partition B. Denote Xa the attrac-

tor associated with the parameter a ∈W. We say that the attractors are semi-continuous

on W if for every a ∈W, there exists a neighborhood O(a) such that for each b ∈ O(a), we

have Xb ⊆ (Xa)ε.

Note that the semi-continuity of the attractor corresponds to the pseudo-Hausdorﬀmetric

d(X, Y ) = sup{d(x, Y ) | x ∈ X}. It is clear that

dH(X, Y ) = max{d(X, Y ), d(Y, X)}.

Conjecture 4.1. If m = d+1, there exists a generic parameter value such that the attractors are semi-continuous in W.

# 5 Piecewise translation maps on tori

In this section, we discuss a special class of piecewise translations of two branches on a two dimensional torus called double rotations. Double rotations were discussed in [17] and [11]. Synchronization properties of random double rotations on tori were studied in [12]. Here we will show some pictures of double rotations with ﬁnite and inﬁnite types.

7

Deﬁnition 5.1. Let T be a two-dimensional torus and v0, v1 are vectors in R2. Consider a

subset R of T. The map f : T → T deﬁned as

f(x) =  x + v0 (mod 1),

if x ∈ R;

x + v1 (mod 1), otherwise

is called a double rotation on T.

In Figure 4, the torus is partitioned into two regions - green and blue. We assign a diﬀerent translation vector to each region. After applying the map, we see that a region from the torus is lost (the red region). In this case, it is the translational image of the green region. Applying the map one more time, we get an additional lost region. Again, this is a translational image of the previous red region. After 500 times, we no longer get any additional lost region. The map is of ﬁnite type and its attractor is the blue part in Figure 5. On the other hands, in Figure 6, we do not get the attractor even after 5000 iterates. The map seems to be of inﬁnite type.

Let V be the space of parameters {v0, v1} with a ﬁxed partition such that the double rota-

tion map fv0,v1 is of ﬁnite type. By computer simulation, we conjecture that the map is of ﬁnite type for almost every parameter. If the map is ﬁnite, we also expect the attractor is semi-continuous with respect to Hausdorﬀdistance. This behavior has already been seen in the previous section.

Conjecture 5.1. V is an open, dense, and full measure subset of the set of all parameters.

Conjecture 5.2. The attractor is semi-continuous with respect to the parameters in V.

Question 5.1. Is it true that the attractor is continuous with respect to the parameters in V?
